name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTKINGDOM_MCQ_Q01 - Classification systems and Plantae exclusions

questiontext.text:
Consider the following three statements regarding plant classification:

Statement I: Fungi and cyanobacteria (blue-green algae) are currently excluded from Kingdom Plantae.

Statement II: Linnaeus's artificial system of classification was based mainly on vegetative characters or the androecium structure.

Statement III: Natural classification systems ignore internal features such as anatomy, ultrastructure, and embryology.

Which of the above statements are correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Evaluation of Plantae Boundaries and Artificial Systems
In the modern understanding of Whittaker's Five Kingdom classification, fungi and cell-walled members of Monera (including cyanobacteria) and Protista are excluded from Kingdom Plantae. Furthermore, Linnaeus's artificial system was indeed based mainly on vegetative characters or on the androecium structure.

Step 2: Evaluation of Natural Classification Systems
Natural classification systems (such as that of Bentham and Hooker) consider both external features and internal features like ultrastructure, anatomy, embryology, and phytochemistry; therefore, the claim that they ignore internal features is incorrect.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Only the first two claims—regarding the exclusion of fungi and cyanobacteria from Plantae and the basis of Linnaeus's artificial system—are correct (I and II only).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTKINGDOM_MCQ_Q02 - General characteristics and associations of algae

questiontext.text:
Consider the following three statements about algae:

Statement I: Algae are chlorophyll-bearing, simple, thalloid, autotrophic, and largely aquatic organisms.

Statement II: Vegetative reproduction in algae commonly takes place by fragmentation.

Statement III: Algae never occur in association with fungi or animals.

Which of the above statements are correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Evaluation of Algal Nature and Vegetative Reproduction
Algae are chlorophyll-bearing, simple, thalloid, autotrophic, and largely aquatic (freshwater and marine) organisms, and they commonly reproduce vegetatively by fragmentation where each fragment develops into a thallus.

Step 2: Evaluation of Algal Associations
Some algae do occur in association with fungi (forming lichens) and animals (for example, growing on the sloth bear); therefore, the claim that they never form such associations is incorrect.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Only the claims regarding the general characteristics of algae and vegetative reproduction by fragmentation are correct (I and II only).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTKINGDOM_MCQ_Q03 - Seed enclosure and size range in seed plants

questiontext.text:
Consider the following three statements regarding seed-bearing plants:

Statement I: In gymnosperms, ovules are not enclosed by any ovary wall and the seeds remain naked.

Statement II: In angiosperms, seeds are enclosed inside fruits.

Statement III: Wolffia is one of the tallest angiosperm trees, reaching over 100 metres in height.

Which of the above statements are correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Evaluation of Seed Enclosure
In gymnosperms, ovules are exposed both before and after fertilisation because they are not enclosed by an ovary wall, resulting in naked seeds. In angiosperms, ovules develop inside an ovary, and post-fertilisation seeds are enclosed within fruits.

Step 2: Evaluation of Angiosperm Size Range
Angiosperms range in size from the smallest flowering plant Wolffia to tall trees of Eucalyptus (over 100 metres); thus, describing Wolffia as a tall tree over 100 metres is incorrect.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Only the claims regarding naked seeds in gymnosperms and fruit-enclosed seeds in angiosperms are correct (I and II only).

questiontext.text:
Consider the following three statements regarding modern taxonomic systems:

Statement I: Phylogenetic classification assumes that organisms belonging to the same taxa have a common ancestor.

Statement II: Cytotaxonomy uses the chemical constituents of the plant to resolve confusions in classification.

Statement III: Numerical taxonomy uses computers to assign numbers and codes to all observable characters, giving each character equal importance.

Which of the above statements are correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Evaluation of Phylogenetic and Numerical Taxonomy
Phylogenetic classification systems are based on evolutionary relationships and assume that organisms in the same taxa share a common ancestor. Numerical taxonomy is carried out using computers by assigning numbers and codes to all observable characters so each character receives equal importance.

Step 2: Evaluation of Cytotaxonomy vs Chemotaxonomy
Cytotaxonomy is based on cytological information such as chromosome number, structure, and behaviour, whereas chemotaxonomy uses chemical constituents of the plant. Thus, attributing chemical constituents to cytotaxonomy is incorrect.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Only the claims regarding phylogenetic classification and numerical taxonomy are correct (I and III only).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTKINGDOM_MCQ_Q05 - Chloroplasts pyrenoids and cell wall of Chlorophyceae

questiontext.text:
Consider the following three statements about Chlorophyceae (green algae):

Statement I: Chlorophyll a and b are localised in definite chloroplasts that may be discoid, plate-like, reticulate, cup-shaped, spiral, or ribbon-shaped.

Statement II: Pyrenoids located in the chloroplasts contain protein besides starch.

Statement III: Green algae have a rigid cell wall made of an inner layer of algin and an outer layer of cellulose.

Which of the above statements are correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Evaluation of Chloroplasts and Pyrenoids
In Chlorophyceae, chlorophyll a and b are localised in definite chloroplasts of varied shapes (discoid, plate-like, reticulate, cup-shaped, spiral, or ribbon-shaped), and most members possess pyrenoids inside chloroplasts containing protein besides starch.

Step 2: Evaluation of Cell Wall Composition
The rigid cell wall of green algae is made of an inner layer of cellulose and an outer layer of pectose—not algin (which is a gelatinous coating in brown algae). Thus, the cell wall claim is incorrect.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Only the claims regarding chloroplast pigments/shapes and pyrenoids are correct (I and II only).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTKINGDOM_MCQ_Q06 - Pigments stored food and zoospores in Phaeophyceae

questiontext.text:
Consider the following three statements about Phaeophyceae (brown algae):

Statement I: Asexual reproduction in most brown algae occurs by non-motile spores lacking flagella.

Statement II: Brown algae vary in colour from olive green to various shades of brown depending on the amount of fucoxanthin present.

Statement III: Food is stored as complex carbohydrates in the form of laminarin or mannitol.

Which of the above statements are correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Evaluation of Asexual Reproduction in Brown Algae
Asexual reproduction in most brown algae is by biflagellate zoospores that are pear-shaped and have two unequal laterally attached flagella, not non-motile spores. Thus, the asexual spore claim is incorrect.

Step 2: Evaluation of Pigments and Stored Food
Brown algae vary in colour from olive green to brown depending on the amount of the xanthophyll pigment fucoxanthin, and their stored food consists of complex carbohydrates such as laminarin or mannitol.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Only the claims regarding fucoxanthin-based colour variation and stored food (laminarin or mannitol) are correct (II and III only).

questiontext.text:
Consider the following three statements about Rhodophyceae (red algae):

Statement I: They are called red algae because of the predominance of the red pigment r-phycoerythrin in their body.

Statement II: Food is stored as floridean starch, which is very similar in structure to amylopectin and glycogen.

Statement III: Sexual reproduction is oogamous and occurs via non-motile gametes.

Which of the above statements are correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Evaluation of Pigment and Stored Food
Members of Rhodophyceae are called red algae due to the predominance of r-phycoerythrin, and they store food as floridean starch, which structurally resembles amylopectin and glycogen.

Step 2: Evaluation of Sexual Reproduction
Flagella are absent in red algae; sexual reproduction is oogamous using non-motile gametes and is accompanied by complex post-fertilisation developments.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
All three claims regarding pigment, stored food, and oogamous reproduction with non-motile gametes are correct (I, II and III).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTKINGDOM_MCQ_Q08 - Gametophyte sex organs and sporophyte dependence in bryophytes

questiontext.text:
Consider the following three statements about bryophytes:

Statement I: The main plant body is a haploid gametophyte attached to the substratum by unicellular or multicellular rhizoids.

Statement II: The male sex organ antheridium produces biflagellate antherozoids.

Statement III: The sporophyte is free-living and nutritionally independent of the gametophyte.

Which of the above statements are correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Evaluation of Bryophyte Gametophyte and Sex Organs
In bryophytes, the main plant body is a haploid gametophyte attached to the substratum by unicellular or multicellular rhizoids, and the multicellular male sex organ (antheridium) produces biflagellate antherozoids.

Step 2: Evaluation of Sporophyte Dependence
The bryophyte sporophyte is not free-living; it remains attached to the photosynthetic gametophyte and derives nourishment from it. Thus, the claim of an independent sporophyte is incorrect.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Only the claims regarding the haploid gametophyte with rhizoids and biflagellate antherozoids from the antheridium are correct (I and II only).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTKINGDOM_MCQ_Q09 - Liverworts and mosses developmental stages

questiontext.text:
Consider the following three statements regarding liverworts and mosses:

Statement I: In mosses, the upright leafy stage develops directly from the zygote as a lateral bud.

Statement II: In liverworts, gemmae are green, multicellular, asexual buds developed in gemma cups on the thalli.

Statement III: In mosses, the protonema stage develops directly from a spore and is creeping, green, branched, and filamentous.

Which of the above statements are correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Evaluation of Moss Leafy Stage Origin
In mosses, the leafy stage develops from the secondary protonema as a lateral bud, not directly from the zygote (the zygote develops into the diploid sporophyte). Hence, the claim about leafy stage origin is incorrect.

Step 2: Evaluation of Gemmae and Protonema
In liverworts, gemmae are green, multicellular asexual buds formed in gemma cups. In mosses, the protonema stage develops directly from a haploid spore as a creeping, green, branched, filamentous stage.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Only the claims regarding gemmae in liverworts and protonema in mosses are correct (II and III only).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTKINGDOM_MCQ_Q10 - Morphology and prothallus of pteridophytes

questiontext.text:
Consider the following three statements about pteridophytes:

Statement I: The main plant body is a sporophyte differentiated into true root, stem, and leaves possessing vascular tissues.

Statement II: Leaves are small (microphylls) as in Selaginella or large (macrophylls) as in ferns.

Statement III: The prothallus requires cool, damp, shady places to grow, and water is needed for transfer of antherozoids.

Which of the above statements are correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Evaluation of Pteridophyte Sporophyte and Leaves
In pteridophytes, the main plant body is a vascular sporophyte with true roots, stems, and leaves. The leaves may be small microphylls (as in Selaginella) or large macrophylls (as in ferns).

Step 2: Evaluation of Prothallus and Fertilisation
Spores germinate to form a small, multicellular, free-living, photosynthetic thalloid gametophyte called a prothallus, which requires cool, damp, shady places, and water is required for the transfer of antherozoids to the archegonium.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
All three claims about pteridophyte sporophyte structure, leaf types, and prothallus/fertilisation requirements are correct (I, II and III).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTKINGDOM_MCQ_Q11 - Heterospory and classification of pteridophytes

questiontext.text:
Consider the following three statements regarding pteridophytes:

Statement I: Selaginella and Salvinia are heterosporous genera producing both megaspores and microspores.

Statement II: Retention of the female gametophyte on the parent sporophyte and embryo development within it is a precursor to the seed habit.

Statement III: Equisetum belongs to class Lycopsida, whereas Psilotum belongs to class Pteropsida.

Which of the above statements are correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Evaluation of Heterospory and Seed Habit Precursor
Selaginella and Salvinia are heterosporous pteridophytes producing large megaspores and small microspores. Their female gametophytes are retained on the parent sporophytes where zygotes develop into young embryos—a key precursor to the seed habit.

Step 2: Evaluation of Pteridophyte Classification
Equisetum belongs to Sphenopsida (not Lycopsida), and Psilotum belongs to Psilopsida (not Pteropsida). Hence, the classification claim is incorrect.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Only the claims regarding heterospory in Selaginella and Salvinia and the precursor to the seed habit are correct (I and II only).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTKINGDOM_MCQ_Q12 - Roots cones and gametophytes of gymnosperms

questiontext.text:
Consider the following three statements about gymnosperms:

Statement I: Pinus has mycorrhizal roots and bears both male and female cones on the same tree.

Statement II: Cycas has coralloid roots associated with N₂-fixing cyanobacteria and bears male cones and megasporophylls on different trees.

Statement III: The pollen grain is a highly reduced male gametophyte, and the multicellular female gametophyte is retained within the megasporangium.

Which of the above statements are correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Evaluation of Pinus and Cycas
In Pinus, roots form fungal associations called mycorrhiza and male and female cones may be borne on the same tree. In Cycas, specialised coralloid roots associate with N₂-fixing cyanobacteria, and male cones and megasporophylls are borne on different trees.

Step 2: Evaluation of Gymnosperm Gametophytes
Gymnosperm gametophytes lack independent free-living existence: microspores develop into highly reduced male gametophytes (pollen grains) within microsporangia, and one megaspore develops into a multicellular female gametophyte retained within the megasporangium.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
All three claims regarding Pinus, Cycas, and gymnosperm gametophytes are correct (I, II and III).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTKINGDOM_MCQ_Q13 - Angiosperm embryo sac and double fertilisation

questiontext.text:
Consider the following three statements regarding angiosperms:

Statement I: Each embryo sac has a three-celled egg apparatus (one egg cell and two synergids), three antipodal cells, and two polar nuclei.

Statement II: After fertilisation, the synergids and antipodals persist and enlarge to form the fruit wall.

Statement III: Triple fusion produces a triploid primary endosperm nucleus (PEN), while syngamy produces a diploid zygote.

Which of the above statements are correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Evaluation of Embryo Sac and Double Fertilisation
An angiosperm embryo sac contains a three-celled egg apparatus (one egg cell and two synergids), three antipodal cells, and two polar nuclei. During double fertilisation, syngamy forms a diploid zygote and triple fusion produces a triploid primary endosperm nucleus (PEN).

Step 2: Evaluation of Post-Fertilisation Fate
After fertilisation, the synergids and antipodals degenerate, while the ovary develops into the fruit and ovules develop into seeds. Thus, the claim that synergids and antipodals form the fruit wall is incorrect.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Only the claims regarding embryo sac structure and double fertilisation products are correct (I and III only).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTKINGDOM_MCQ_Q14 - Life cycle patterns and exceptions in plants

questiontext.text:
Consider the following three statements regarding plant life cycles:

Statement I: Volvox and Spirogyra exhibit a haplontic life cycle in which the sporophytic generation is represented only by the one-celled zygote.

Statement II: Fucus is an alga that exhibits a diplontic life cycle, whereas Ectocarpus, Polysiphonia, and kelps are haplo-diplontic.

Statement III: Both bryophytes and pteridophytes exhibit a haplo-diplontic life cycle with the diploid sporophyte as the dominant phase.

Which of the above statements are correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Evaluation of Algal Life Cycles
Volvox and Spirogyra follow a haplontic life cycle where the one-celled zygote is the only sporophytic phase. Among algal exceptions, Fucus is diplontic, while Ectocarpus, Polysiphonia, and kelps are haplo-diplontic.

Step 2: Evaluation of Bryophyte vs Pteridophyte Dominant Phase
Although both bryophytes and pteridophytes are haplo-diplontic, bryophytes have a dominant haploid gametophyte, whereas pteridophytes have a dominant diploid sporophyte. Thus, claiming both have a dominant diploid sporophyte is incorrect.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Only the claims regarding haplontic algae and algal life cycle exceptions are correct (I and II only).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTKINGDOM_MCQ_Q15 - Meiosis and ploidy across plant groups

questiontext.text:
Consider the following three statements regarding meiosis and ploidy in plants:

Statement I: In gymnosperms, the megaspore mother cell divides mitotically to form four diploid megaspores.

Statement II: In bryophytes, meiosis takes place within the capsule of the sporophyte to produce haploid spores.

Statement III: The primary endosperm nucleus in a dicot is triploid (3n), whereas a leaf cell of a moss and a prothallus cell of a fern are haploid (n).

Which of the above statements are correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Evaluation of Gymnosperm Megasporogenesis
In gymnosperms, the megaspore mother cell divides meiotically (not mitotically) to form four haploid megaspores. Hence, the claim of mitotic division forming diploid megaspores is incorrect.

Step 2: Evaluation of Bryophyte Meiosis and Ploidy Levels
In bryophytes (liverworts and mosses), meiosis occurs inside the capsule of the sporophyte to produce haploid spores. Furthermore, the dicot primary endosperm nucleus is triploid (3n) from triple fusion, while moss leaf cells and fern prothallus cells belong to the gametophyte and are haploid (n).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Only the claims regarding meiosis in the bryophyte capsule and the ploidy levels of dicot PEN, moss leaf cell, and fern prothallus are correct (II and III only).
